answer: Black and Hispanic (compared to White). In a logistic regression of BA DEGREE COMPLETED on SAMPLE_RACE in the NLS data, the factor (log-odds coefficient) for the combined Black+Hispanic pair relative to White is ≈ -0.96 to -0.97 (MLE -0.974; Firth bias-corrected -0.966), matching the reported value -0.9568. This is the only two-races-vs-third pairing whose factor is near -0.9568; the other groupings ({White,Hispanic} vs Black = -0.876 and {White,Black} vs Hispanic = -0.722) and the single-race-vs-White contrasts (Black vs White = -1.006, Hispanic vs White = -0.924) do not match. The negative factor means Black/Hispanic respondents have lower odds of completing a BA degree than White respondents.

payload.hypothesis: In the NLS dataset, the factor (log-odds coefficient) of BA DEGREE COMPLETED of -0.9568 corresponds to the pair of races Black and Hispanic, compared to the other race, White. In a logistic regression of BA DEGREE COMPLETED on SAMPLE_RACE, the combined Black+Hispanic group has a log-odds coefficient of about -0.96 to -0.97 relative to White (MLE -0.974; Firth bias-corrected -0.966), the only two-races-vs-third pairing near -0.9568. The negative factor indicates Black and Hispanic respondents have lower odds of completing a BA degree than White respondents.
payload.workflow: Loaded nls_ses_processed.csv (8773 x 8, no missing). Treated 'factor' as the log-odds coefficient from a logistic regression of the binary outcome BA DEGREE COMPLETED on race. (1) Fitted the three 'two-races-vs-third' logistic models (pair combined vs the remaining race) with MLE and Firth bias-corrected estimation. (2) Fitted the three-group reference-coded model to get the three pairwise log-odds contrasts. (3) Ranked all 'pair vs third' factors by |value - (-0.9568)|; {Black,Hispanic} vs White was closest (MLE -0.974, Firth -0.966). (4) Sensitivity: re-fit the {Black,Hispanic} vs White model across all 32 covariate subsets (SES, ABILITY, PERCENTILE, FAMILY SIZE, SEX); the unadjusted model is closest to the target, while adding covariates moves the factor toward 0/positive and makes the race estimates unstable, supporting a simple unadjusted logistic specification. Concluded the pair is Black and Hispanic vs White.
